q: What kinds of questions come up in a product analytics or product data science interview?
plain: Expect five kinds of question. A technical screen tests SQL and basic statistics. A product sense question asks you to define success for a feature, such as how you would measure a new short video tab. A root cause question hands you a metric that moved and asks why. An estimation question asks for a rough number reasoned from scratch. A case round gives you data and asks for a recommendation. A typical loop at a consumer app mixes several, for example a SQL window function problem followed by 'daily rides fell 8 percent last Tuesday, investigate'.
deep:
One useful taxonomy comes from chapter 6 of the product data science interview book. You are asked to **measure something for the first time**, to **find the root cause** of a recent metric change, to estimate a **counterfactual impact** (what would have happened without a system or change), or to weigh a **trade off** between a benefit and a cost.

Around those four sit the other rounds:

| Round | Example prompt | What it tests | Where it lives |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SQL | Retention by signup cohort | Joins, windows, aggregation | SQL module |
| Experiments and statistics | Is a 0.3 point lift real? | Power, variance, pitfalls | Experimentation module |
| Product sense | How would you measure Stories? | Metric design, user empathy | North star, metrics, product sense sections |
| Root cause | DAU fell 10 percent | Structured diagnosis | Diagnosing a metric drop |
| Estimation | How many rides per day in a city? | Assumptions, arithmetic | Estimation |
| BI tools | LOD expression, DAX measure | Tool fluency | Excel, Tableau and Power BI |
| Behavioural | A time data changed a decision | Influence, exec communication | Communicating to executives |

Not every company runs every round. Product analyst and BI loops lean on SQL, dashboards and communication. Product data scientist loops add experimentation depth. Ask the recruiter for the exact loop and prepare that mix.
say: There are really five kinds. A technical screen with SQL and basic statistics, a product sense question where I define success for a feature, a root cause question where a metric moved and I explain why, an estimation question where I reason my way to a rough number, and a case round where I get data and make a recommendation. What I keep in mind is that three of the five are open ended, so interviewers care less about the final answer and more about whether I structure the problem, state my assumptions, and finish with a clear recommendation.
must_mention: root cause of a metric change

followups.q: Which of these is hardest to prepare for?
followups.a: Root cause and product sense, because there is no single right answer. Practise them out loud with a fixed structure.

followups.q: Where do experiments fit in?
followups.a: Sometimes as their own round, sometimes as a follow up inside product sense: 'how would you test it?' The experimentation module has the detail.

traps: Treating every question as a SQL or modelling question and skipping the business framing.

q: How do product analyst, BI analyst and product data scientist interviews differ?
plain: Titles overlap, but the emphasis differs. A product analyst works with product managers on metrics, funnels and experiment readouts, so expect product sense and SQL. A BI analyst builds and maintains reporting for the business, so expect SQL, dashboards in Tableau or Power BI, Excel and data modelling. A product data scientist does the analyst work plus deeper experiment design, causal inference and some modelling. Read the job post for tool names and ask the recruiter for the rounds. A post that lists Tableau and stakeholder reporting points to a BI loop; one that lists A/B testing and causal inference points to a data science loop.
deep:
Treat this as a tendency, not a rule. The same title means different things at different companies, so confirm the loop before you spend a week on the wrong material.

| | Product analyst | BI analyst | Product data scientist |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main job | Explain and improve product metrics | Build trusted reporting for a business function | Measure causal impact and build models for product decisions |
| Heaviest rounds | Product sense, SQL, root cause | SQL, dashboards, Excel, data modelling | Experiments, statistics, product sense, some ML |
| Typical tools | SQL, Python or R, an experimentation platform | SQL, Tableau or Power BI, Excel, a warehouse | SQL, Python, causal inference libraries |
| Typical output | A recommendation and a metric readout | A dashboard, a recurring report, a metric definition | An experiment design, a model, a causal estimate |
| Failure mode | Lists metrics with no decision | Builds charts nobody trusts or uses | Over engineers when a segment cut would do |

What overlaps: every one of these roles is asked to define a metric precisely, find out why it moved, and say what to do next, in plain language. That shared core is what this module covers. SQL and experiment design have their own modules.
say: They overlap, but the weight is different. A product analyst sits next to product managers, so the loop is product sense, SQL and root cause on metrics. A BI analyst owns reporting, so I'd expect SQL, Tableau or Power BI, Excel and data modelling questions. A product data scientist does the analyst work plus deeper experimentation, causal inference and sometimes modelling. Titles vary by company, so I read the job description for tool names, ask the recruiter what each round covers, and then spend my prep time in proportion to that.
must_mention: product analyst: metrics, funnels, product sense
BI analyst: SQL, dashboards, Excel, modelling
data scientist: experiments and causal inference

followups.q: How would you find out what the loop covers?
followups.a: Ask the recruiter for the round list and the tools, and read the job post for tool names such as Tableau, Power BI, dbt or an experimentation platform.

followups.q: What skill is common to all three?
followups.a: Defining a metric precisely, explaining why it moved, and communicating a recommendation to a non technical audience.

traps: Preparing only for modelling when the role is analytics and reporting.

q: How should you structure your answer to any open ended analytics question?
plain: Use the same five moves every time. First, restate the goal and ask clarifying questions about the metric, the users and the time frame. Second, say your structure out loud as three or four buckets so the interviewer can steer. Third, work through the buckets in priority order, with rough numbers. Fourth, wrap up with the answer first, then the reason and the risks. Fifth, check in after each bucket. For a question about falling signups you might say, 'I will check the data first, then split by platform and country, then walk the funnel, then propose fixes', and only then start.
deep:
**The five moves**

1. **Restate and clarify (about 3 minutes in a 30 minute round).** Pin the metric down: numerator, denominator, window, population. Ask how big the change is, when it started, who noticed it, and what is already ruled out. Ask what business decision rides on the answer. If the interviewer will not answer, state an assumption out loud and continue; say you would verify it.
2. **Structure (about 1 to 2 minutes).** Offer buckets that do not overlap and together cover the problem. Say them in one breath, then ask "does that cover what you care about?"
3. **Analyse in priority order.** For each bucket say what you would look at, what you expect to see under each hypothesis, and what you would do next. Size things with rough numbers so the interviewer hears judgement, not a checklist.
4. **Synthesise.** Answer first. Then the two or three facts that support it, the recommendation, your confidence, the main risk, and what evidence would change your mind.
5. **Interact.** At each fork offer a choice ("I can go to the funnel or to segments next, which do you prefer?"). Interviewers often steer you to the part they want to test.

**Template sentences.** "Before I answer, let me make sure I understand the metric." "I will look at four things, in this order." "My recommendation is X, and I am fairly confident because Y; I would be wrong if Z."

The time split is a suggestion, not a rule. The point is that every question gets a clarification, a visible structure and a closing recommendation.
say: I use the same five moves every time. First I restate the goal and ask clarifying questions about the metric definition, the size of the change and the time frame. Then I say my structure out loud in three or four buckets so the interviewer can steer me. I work through the buckets in priority order with rough numbers, and I check in at each fork. At the end I give the answer first, then the evidence, a recommendation, my confidence and what would change my mind. If the interviewer won't answer a clarifying question, I state an assumption and keep moving.
must_mention: answer first, then evidence and recommendation

followups.q: What if the interviewer refuses to clarify?
followups.a: State the assumption explicitly, proceed, and say how you would verify it with real data.

followups.q: How long should the structure take to state?
followups.a: One to two minutes. If it takes longer it is a list, not a structure.

traps: Diving into the first hypothesis without saying how it fits a plan.
Ending without a recommendation.

q: What do interviewers actually score in a product analytics case, and what sinks candidates?
plain: Interviewers usually score four things: how well you structure an open problem, whether your business and product judgement is sound, whether your numbers and logic hold up, and whether you communicate clearly. They are rarely hunting for one right answer. Candidates sink themselves by skipping data verification, listing a dozen causes in no order, using metrics with no definition, forgetting a counter metric, or never giving a recommendation. For example, answering 'DAU dropped' with a long list of guesses scores worse than checking the logging first and then narrowing by platform.
deep:
**A typical rubric (a synthesis of how these rounds are commonly graded, not an official company rubric)**

| Dimension | Strong signal | Weak signal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | Names buckets, orders them, revisits the plan | Free association, no order |
| Product and business judgement | Ties the metric to a user need and a business goal, sizes the impact | Metric soup with no goal |
| Quantitative reasoning | Defines ratios precisely, sanity checks magnitudes, notes denominators | Mixes up rates and counts, ignores scale |
| Communication | Answer first, plain words, checks understanding | Long preamble, jargon |
| Collaboration under ambiguity | Asks sharp clarifying questions, takes hints | Defensive, ignores the interviewer |

**Common ways to lose points**

- Naming a root cause before checking that the data is correct.
- An unordered list of 12 hypotheses. Order them by likelihood and by cost to check.
- A success metric with no definition of "active", "conversion" or the window.
- No counter metric, so the proposed metric is easy to game.
- Ignoring magnitude: a 3 percent drop in a metric that is 0.2 percent of revenue may not matter.
- Treating the interviewer as an opponent. The product data science book advises engaging them and asking how they see the problem, even when the interviewer is unhelpful.
- Ending on analysis with no decision.
say: Mostly four things: structure on an open problem, business and product judgement, whether my numbers and logic hold up, and how clearly I communicate. There's rarely one right answer, so they're watching how I handle uncertainty. The ways people sink themselves are skipping data verification, listing a dozen causes with no order, using metrics with no definition, forgetting a counter metric, and never giving a recommendation. So I check that the data is right first, order my hypotheses by likelihood and cost to test, size the impact, and finish with a recommendation and a confidence level.

followups.q: What is the single most common mistake?
followups.a: Explaining a metric move before verifying the data is real, since logging and pipeline issues are a frequent cause.

followups.q: What if the interviewer disagrees with my approach?
followups.a: Ask for their view, say what you gain by their path, and switch if it is reasonable. Collaboration is part of the score.

traps: Listing every possible cause with no prioritisation.

q: What do DAU, WAU and MAU measure, and why must you define 'active' before quoting them?
plain: DAU, WAU and MAU count distinct users who were active on a given day, in the last 7 days, and in the last 28 or 30 days. 'Active' is a choice the team makes: opening the app, logging in, firing any event, or doing a core action like sending a message. A messaging app might report 10 million DAU if opens count and 6 million if a sent message counts. Whenever you quote one of these numbers, say which event counts, which window, which time zone, and whether bots, staff and duplicate devices were removed.
deep:
**Definitions.** For a day $t$,

$$\text{DAU}_t = \left|\{u : u \text{ has at least one qualifying event on day } t\}\right|$$

WAU and MAU use a window of 7 and 28 (or 30) days ending on $t$. Each user counts once however many days they were active.

**Choices that change the number**

- **Qualifying event.** Any event, a foreground session, or a core action. A push notification being delivered should never count as activity. For a marketplace, a core action definition ("monthly active buyers") is usually more honest than "opened the app".
- **Identity.** User id, device id or cookie. Logged out traffic and multiple devices per person move the count in opposite directions. State which you use.
- **Time zone.** Calendar day in UTC versus in the user's local time. A global product on UTC days splits one evening of usage across two days.
- **Exclusions.** Bots, employees, test accounts, fraud.
- **Window.** A rolling 28 day window contains exactly four of each weekday, so it does not wobble with weekday mix. A 30 day or calendar month window does.
- **Average versus end of period.** Monthly "average DAU" and "MAU at month end" answer different questions.

**Discipline.** Version the definition. If the definition changes, the trend line breaks, so annotate it or restate history.
say: They count distinct users who were active on a day, in the last seven days, and in the last 28 or 30 days. The key point is that 'active' is a definition, not a fact. It might mean opened the app, logged in, or did a core action like sent a message, and those can differ by 40 percent or more. So whenever I quote a number I say which event counts, the window, the time zone, and whether bots, staff and duplicate devices are removed. I also prefer a 28 day window because it holds exactly four of each weekday.

followups.q: Why 28 days rather than a calendar month?
followups.a: A 28 day window always contains four of each weekday, so the metric does not move because a month has five weekends.

followups.q: Device level or user level?
followups.a: User level is closer to the question. Device level is easier to measure and overcounts people with several devices, so state which one you use.

traps: Quoting DAU without saying what counts as active.

q: What is stickiness, how do you compute DAU over MAU, and what does 30 percent mean?
plain: Stickiness is the share of monthly users who show up on a typical day, computed as average DAU divided by MAU. With 120,000 DAU and 400,000 MAU it is 30 percent. That means the average monthly user was active about 9 days out of 30. A related ratio, DAU divided by WAU, gives 48 percent with 250,000 WAU, which means about 3.4 days out of 7. Higher means more habitual, but what counts as good depends on how often the product is naturally used.
deep:
**Formula.**

$$\text{stickiness} = \frac{\text{average DAU over the period}}{\text{MAU}}$$

**Why it means "days active per month".** If $N$ users were active at least once in a $D$ day month and user $i$ was active on $d_i$ of those days, then average DAU is $\sum_i d_i / D$ and MAU is $N$. So

$$\frac{\text{avg DAU}}{\text{MAU}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \frac{d_i}{D} = \frac{\bar d}{D}$$

the average fraction of days a monthly user is active. I checked this identity on 2,000 simulated users and both sides agreed (0.3194). A ratio of 0.30 over 30 days is 9 active days.

**Worked numbers.** DAU 120,000, WAU 250,000, MAU 400,000.

| Ratio | Value | Reads as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DAU / MAU | 30% | 9 days of 30 |
| DAU / WAU | 48% | 3.4 days of 7 |
| WAU / MAU | 62.5% | most monthly users come back within a week |

**Variants.** DAU/WAU for products with a weekly rhythm, WAU/MAU for a weekly product, and L7 or L28 (the count of days a user was active in the last 7 or 28), which gives a full distribution instead of one ratio.

**Caveat.** There is no universal good number. Compare to your own history and to products with similar natural frequency, and read it with the next card on when it misleads.
say: Stickiness is average DAU divided by MAU, so it tells me what share of my monthly users show up on a typical day. With 120,000 daily and 400,000 monthly actives it's 30 percent, which works out to the average monthly user being active about 9 days out of 30. That interpretation is exact, because average DAU over MAU is the average fraction of days each monthly user was active. The caveat is that a good ratio depends on the product's natural frequency, so I compare it to my own history and to similar products rather than to a universal benchmark.
must_mention: exact identity: mean active days over days in month

followups.q: What does DAU/WAU of 48 percent mean?
followups.a: The average weekly user is active about 3.4 days of 7.

followups.q: What is L28?
followups.a: For each user, the number of days active in the last 28. Its histogram shows how engagement is distributed, not just the average.

traps: Comparing stickiness across products with different natural frequency.

q: When is DAU over MAU a misleading engagement measure?
plain: It misleads in two ways. First, it assumes daily use is the goal, but a tax filing app or a travel site is healthy with a few visits a year, so a low ratio means nothing. Second, the ratio moves when the denominator moves. If DAU is 100,000 and MAU is 500,000 the ratio is 20 percent. If 100,000 casual monthly users leave, MAU falls to 400,000 and stickiness rises to 25 percent even though the product lost a fifth of its users. Look at the distribution of days active, not one ratio.
deep:
**Failure 1: wrong cadence.** The ratio assumes the right behaviour is daily. For a grocery app a weekly cadence is healthy, and for a tax product a yearly one is. Define the product's natural cadence and measure the share of users who meet it (for example, share of monthly actives with at least 4 active days).

**Failure 2: denominator effect.** Stickiness is a ratio of two moving numbers.

| | DAU | MAU | DAU / MAU |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Before | 100,000 | 500,000 | 20% |
| After 100k casual users stop appearing | 100,000 | 400,000 | 25% |

The ratio improved 5 points while the user base shrank 20%. The product got worse on reach and "better" on stickiness.

**Failure 3: averages hide shape.** Two products can share a 30% ratio, one with every user active 9 days and one with a core of daily users plus a long tail of one day visitors. They need different strategies.

**What to do instead**

- Plot the **L28 histogram** (users by number of active days in the last 28) and compare its shape over time. Watch the mass at 1 day (tourists) and at 20 or more days (core).
- Track **reach** (MAU) and **frequency** (days per active user) as separate lines.
- Choose the cadence from product logic and data on how often retained users come back.
say: DAU over MAU misleads when daily use isn't the goal, like a tax or travel product, where a low ratio is normal. It also misleads because it's a ratio of two moving numbers. With 100,000 DAU and 500,000 MAU the ratio is 20 percent. If 100,000 casual users disappear, MAU drops to 400,000 and the ratio jumps to 25 percent, even though I lost a fifth of my users. So I track reach and frequency separately, and I look at the histogram of days active over the last 28 days instead of one ratio.
must_mention: assumes daily use is the goal
denominator effect: casual users leaving raises the ratio

followups.q: How would you measure engagement for a product used a few times a year?
followups.a: Pick its natural cadence, such as one visit per quarter, and measure the share of customers who meet it plus repeat completion of the core task.

followups.q: What would you plot instead?
followups.a: The histogram of days active in the last 28, tracked over time, alongside MAU.

traps: Celebrating a stickiness increase without checking whether MAU fell.

q: What is activation, and how do you define an activation metric for a new product?
plain: Activation is the moment a new user first gets real value from the product, measured as the share of signups who complete a key action within a set window. If 1,000 users sign up for a project app and 380 create and share a first project within 7 days, 7 day activation is 38 percent. You find the action by comparing what retained users did early on with what churned users did. It must reflect value the user received, such as a first shared project, not a vanity step like finishing the welcome screens.
deep:
**Definition.**

$$\text{activation rate} = \frac{\text{signups in the cohort who reach the activation event within } T}{\text{signups in the cohort}}$$

**How to choose the event and window**

1. Start from product logic and user research: what is the first moment the user obtains the benefit they came for? For a messaging app, a first reply received. For a project tool, a first shared project.
2. Check data. For each candidate event (and threshold, for example 3 or more), compare retention at day 30 for users who did it within the first week against users who did not.
3. Prefer an event that is early, reachable for a large share of users, strongly linked to retention, and something product changes can nudge.
4. Pick the window $T$ from the distribution of time to first action. If 80% of eventual activators act within 3 days, a 7 day window captures nearly all of them without waiting.
5. Validate causally with an experiment, because users who do effortful things are already more motivated (the next card).

**Quality checks.** Activation should move before retention does, and a rise in activation with flat retention means the event is not really value.

**Example.** 1,000 signups, 380 activated in 7 days: 38%. Report it by signup cohort and by acquisition channel, since paid and organic users activate at different rates.
say: Activation is the first time a new user actually gets value, measured as the share of signups who do a key action within a set window. For a project tool, say 380 of 1,000 signups create and share a first project within a week, so seven day activation is 38 percent. I find the action by comparing what retained users did in their first days with what churned users did, then pick one that's early, reachable, and strongly tied to retention. Then I confirm with an experiment, because motivated users do more of everything and that can fake a link.
must_mention: share of signups reaching a value moment in a window
found by comparing retained versus churned early behaviour

followups.q: How do you choose the window?
followups.a: From the distribution of time to first action: choose the point where most eventual activators have acted.

followups.q: Activation is rising but retention is flat. What does that suggest?
followups.a: The activation event is probably not delivering value, or the extra activators are low intent users.

traps: Defining activation as completing onboarding screens.

q: You pick 'adds 3 friends in 7 days' as an activation event. How do you know it causes retention?
plain: You do not know from the data alone. Users who add three friends are more motivated, so their higher retention is partly selection. Suppose 20 percent of users hit the threshold and keep at 52 percent at day 30, while everyone else keeps at 9.5 percent, a 42.5 point gap. Then you randomise a nudge that suggests friends. Day 30 retention rises 2 points, from 18 to 20 percent, and the share reaching three friends rises 11 points. The effect per induced user is 2 divided by 11, about 18 points, well below the 42.5 point gap.
deep:
**The trap.** Retention among users who did X versus did not is an observational comparison. Motivated users do X and also stay. The gap overstates what X causes.

**Observational numbers.** Overall D30 retention is 18%. Twenty percent of users reach 3 or more friends and 52% of them are retained. Then the other 80% must be retained at

$$\frac{0.18 - 0.20 \times 0.52}{0.80} = 0.095$$

so the gap is $0.52 - 0.095 = 0.425$, or 42.5 points.

**Randomised nudge.** Randomly show some new users a friend suggestion step. Results: D30 retention rises from 18% to 20% (the intent to treat effect, 2 points), and the share who reach 3 friends rises from 20% to 31% (the first stage, 11 points).

**Wald estimate (a simple instrumental variable).** If the nudge affects retention only by moving people to 3 friends,

$$\text{effect per induced user} = \frac{\text{ITT on retention}}{\text{ITT on reaching threshold}} = \frac{0.02}{0.11} \approx 0.182$$

About 18 points, versus the 42.5 point observational gap. The people the nudge moves are marginal users, so this is a local effect (for compliers), not the effect for everyone.

```python
obs_share, obs_hit, base = 0.20, 0.52, 0.18
others = (base - obs_share * obs_hit) / (1 - obs_share)
print("D30 of users who did not hit 3 friends:", round(others, 3))
print("observational gap:", round(obs_hit - others, 3))
itt = 0.20 - 0.18          # D30 lift from randomised nudge
first_stage = 0.31 - 0.20  # extra users reaching 3 friends because of the nudge
print("effect per induced user:", round(itt / first_stage, 3))
```

**Conclusion to say aloud.** The threshold is a useful signal and a target for design, but the size of its causal effect is much smaller than the raw gap, and it should be sized from the experiment, not from the correlation. The assumption to name: the nudge changes retention only through the friend count (the exclusion restriction).
say: From the data alone I don't. Users who add three friends are already more motivated, so part of the retention gap is selection. In my example about 20 percent hit the threshold and retain at 52 percent at day 30, versus 9.5 percent for the rest, a gap of 42.5 points. To get a causal read I'd randomise a nudge. If it lifts retention by 2 points and lifts the share reaching three friends by 11 points, the effect per induced user is about 18 points. That's the number I'd use for planning, with the caveat that it applies to marginal users.
must_mention: observational gap is confounded by motivation
intent to treat divided by first stage
effect per induced user is smaller than the gap
assumption: nudge works only through the mediator

followups.q: What assumption does the Wald estimate need?
followups.a: That the nudge changes retention only by changing the friend count (exclusion), and that it pushes people in one direction (monotonicity).

followups.q: Who does the 18 point effect apply to?
followups.a: Users the nudge actually moved, called compliers, not necessarily all users.

traps: Reporting the 42.5 point gap as the causal effect of adding friends.

q: How do you measure engagement beyond DAU: frequency, intensity and depth?
plain: DAU says how many people showed up, not what they did. Frequency is how often a user returns, such as days active per month. Intensity is how much they do when they show up, such as minutes or actions per active day. Depth is how much of the product they use, such as the number of distinct features or content types. For a video app that could be sessions per active user, minutes per session, and the share of users who watch three or more different shows. Each can mislead alone: time spent rises when a product is slow or confusing.
deep:
| Dimension | Example metrics | How it can mislead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frequency | Days active per month, sessions per active user | Notifications can inflate sessions without value |
| Intensity | Minutes per session, actions per active day | Slow or confusing flows raise time spent |
| Depth | Distinct features used, content types consumed | Feature checklists reward clutter |
| Quality | Task success rate, satisfaction survey, repeat completion of the core job | Surveys have response bias |

**Practical rules**

- **Pick a core action** that represents value (a ride completed, a message sent, a recipe cooked) and count users and frequency of that action.
- **Report distributions, not only means.** Usage is skewed: a few power users dominate the mean. Report the median and the 90th percentile as well.
- **Composite scores** (for example a weighted sum of posts, replies, likes and views) are fine for a headline if the weights are justified, but always keep the components visible. In the forum example in the product data science book, the headline engagement score dropped 3 standard deviations, and only the components showed that likes and replies were the ones that fell.
- **Normalise carefully.** Per user, per session and per day answer different questions. Name the denominator.
say: I split engagement into frequency, intensity and depth. Frequency is how often someone comes back, like days active per month. Intensity is how much they do per visit, like minutes or core actions per active day. Depth is how much of the product they use, like distinct features or content types. For a video app I'd look at sessions per active user, minutes per session, and the share watching three or more different shows. I report medians and the 90th percentile, since power users skew the mean, and I keep composite scores split into components.
must_mention: pick a core action that represents value

followups.q: Why can time spent mislead?
followups.a: It rises when the product is slow or confusing, so pair it with task success or satisfaction.

followups.q: Why report percentiles?
followups.a: Usage is heavily skewed, so a mean mostly reflects the few heaviest users.

traps: Using time spent as a proxy for value with no quality check.

q: What is retention, and what is the difference between N day, unbounded and bracket retention?
plain: Retention is the share of a group of users who come back after some time. N day retention counts only users active on exactly day N after signup. Unbounded retention counts users active on day N or any later day. Bracket retention counts users active at any point in a range, such as days 7 to 13. With 10 users, day 7 exact might be 40 percent, day 7 or later 70 percent, and days 7 to 13 60 percent. Pick the type that matches how often the product is naturally used.
deep:
**Setup.** Take a cohort (users who signed up in the same period). Let day 0 be signup. Retention at some age is the fraction of the cohort that qualifies.

| Type | Counts a user if they were active... | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| N day (classic, strict) | exactly on day N | Daily use products such as messaging |
| Unbounded (return on or after day N) | on day N or any later day | Products with irregular use, to see who has not churned |
| Bracket (range) | in a window, such as days 7 to 13 | Weekly use products, such as week 2 retention |

**Worked example.** Ten users, with days since signup on which each was active:

```python
import pandas as pd

activity = {1: [0, 1, 2, 7, 8, 14], 2: [0, 1, 3], 3: [0, 7], 4: [0], 5: [0, 2, 6, 9, 12],
            6: [0, 1, 7, 8, 9], 7: [0, 8, 10], 8: [0, 1], 9: [0, 3, 7], 10: [0, 14]}
events = pd.DataFrame([(u, d) for u, days in activity.items() for d in days],
                      columns=["user", "day"])   # day = days since signup
n = events["user"].nunique()
print("D1 exact     ", events.query("day == 1")["user"].nunique() / n)
print("D7 exact     ", events.query("day == 7")["user"].nunique() / n)
print("D7 unbounded ", events.query("day >= 7")["user"].nunique() / n)
print("days 7 to 13 ", events.query("7 <= day <= 13")["user"].nunique() / n)
```

Output: D1 exact 0.4, D7 exact 0.4, D7 unbounded 0.7, days 7 to 13 0.6. Same data, three different "day 7 retention" numbers, so always say which one.

- Unbounded retention never goes up with age and is always at least the exact figure at that age.
- Retention can be defined on any action, not only app open. "Retained on the core action" is usually more useful than "opened the app".
- Compare cohorts at the same age, never at the same calendar date (the cohorts section covers this).

On the same ten users I get 40 percent for day 7 exact, 70 percent for day 7 or later, and 60 percent for days 7 to 13. q: How do you read a retention curve, and what do its shapes tell you?
plain: A retention curve plots the share of a cohort still active at each age. A curve that flattens at a plateau, such as 100, 40, 30, 26, 24, 23, 23 percent, means a core group has found lasting value. A curve that keeps sliding toward zero, such as 100, 35, 20, 12, 7, 4, 2 percent, means the product is a leaky bucket and more acquisition will not fix it. A curve that dips and later rises, a smile, means users come back, for example seasonally. Overlay cohorts to see whether newer ones do better.
deep:
**Three shapes**

| Shape | Example (percent retained by age) | Reading | Typical action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Flattens | 100, 40, 30, 26, 24, 23, 23 | A core cohort finds durable value, a necessary sign of product market fit | Raise the plateau, improve acquisition quality |
| Decays to zero | 100, 35, 20, 12, 7, 4, 2 | Leaky bucket: users try it and leave | Fix value delivery and activation before spending on acquisition |
| Smile | 100, 30, 18, 15, 17, 22 | Users return, often seasonal or triggered by an event | Find the trigger, lean into resurrection |

**What to look for**

- **The early drop.** The steepest fall is usually between day 0 and day 1 or week 0 and week 1. That is an activation problem.
- **The plateau height.** Lifting it needs a better core product. Lifting the early drop needs better onboarding.
- **Cohort overlay.** Plot each signup cohort as its own line against age. If recent cohorts sit higher, the product is improving. If they sit lower while the blended number looks fine, the mix of users is changing.
- **Segment splits.** Overlay by acquisition channel or platform. A blended curve is a weighted average of different curves.
- **Absolute levels.** What counts as a good plateau depends on how often the product is naturally used, so compare with your own history and with similar products.
say: I plot the share of a cohort still active against age and look at the shape. If it flattens at a plateau, say 100, 40, 30, 26, 24, 23 percent, a core group has found lasting value, which is a good sign. If it keeps falling toward zero, it's a leaky bucket and buying more users won't fix it. A smile means users come back, often seasonally. Then I overlay cohorts to see whether newer ones do better, and split by channel, because a blended curve is a weighted average of different groups. The early drop points to activation, and the plateau height points to the core product.

followups.q: Which is easier to move, the early drop or the plateau?
followups.a: The early drop, usually through onboarding. A higher plateau needs the core product to deliver more lasting value.

followups.q: Why overlay cohorts?
followups.a: To see whether new cohorts retain better than old ones, and to avoid a blended curve hiding a mix change.

q: What is churn rate, and how do you convert between monthly and annual churn?
plain: Churn rate is the share of customers you had at the start of a period who are gone by its end. If you start a month with 1,000 customers and lose 50, monthly churn is 5 percent. Annual churn is not 12 times the monthly figure, because the survivors keep shrinking. Surviving 12 months at 95 percent each month is 0.95 to the power 12, about 54 percent, so annual churn is 46 percent, not 60 percent. Churn can be counted in customers or in revenue, and the two can tell different stories.
deep:
**Definitions** (following the a16z startup metrics article)

- **Unit (logo) churn** = customers lost in the month / customers at the end of the prior month.
- **Gross dollar churn** = recurring revenue lost to cancellations and downgrades in the month / recurring revenue at the start of the month.
- **Net dollar churn** = (revenue lost - revenue gained from expansion of existing customers) / starting revenue. It can be negative when upsell outweighs losses, but it blends two effects, so the article notes it understates losses.

**Compounding.** With constant monthly churn $c$, the probability a customer survives $n$ months is $(1-c)^n$.

$$\text{annual churn} = 1 - (1 - c)^{12}$$

For $c = 0.05$: survival $0.95^{12} = 0.5404$, annual churn $0.4596$. Multiplying instead gives $12 \times 0.05 = 0.60$, which overstates losses by about 14 points.

**Going the other way.** Monthly churn from annual churn $a$ is $1 - (1 - a)^{1/12}$.

**Customers versus revenue.** If small customers churn more than large ones, logo churn is high but revenue churn is low. Report both, and by segment.
say: Churn rate is the share of customers at the start of a period who are gone by the end. Start with 1,000, lose 50, and monthly churn is 5 percent. To annualise, I don't multiply by twelve, I compound the survivors. Surviving 12 months at 95 percent a month is 0.95 to the twelfth, about 54 percent, so annual churn is about 46 percent, not 60. I also separate logo churn from revenue churn, because if small customers leave more than big ones the customer count looks worse than the revenue does.
must_mention: annual is one minus survival compounded
5 percent monthly is about 46 percent annual

followups.q: What is gross versus net dollar churn?
followups.a: Gross counts only revenue lost to cancellations and downgrades. Net also subtracts expansion revenue, so it can be negative.

followups.q: How do you get monthly churn from an annual figure?
followups.a: One minus the twelfth root of annual survival, so 1 minus (1 minus annual churn) to the power one twelfth.

traps: Multiplying monthly churn by 12 to get annual churn.

q: Why is average customer lifetime one over churn, and when is that estimate wrong?
plain: If a customer has the same chance c of leaving each month, the expected lifetime is 1 over c months. At 5 percent monthly churn that is 20 months. It is wrong when customers differ. Say 60 percent of customers churn at 2 percent a month and 40 percent churn at 10 percent. Blended churn starts at 5.2 percent, so the formula says 19.2 months. The true average is 0.6 times 50 plus 0.4 times 10, which is 34 months, because the fast churners leave early and the loyal group dominates later.
deep:
**Derivation (constant churn).** Let the customer leave each month with probability $c$. The lifetime $L$ in months is geometric: $P(L = k) = (1-c)^{k-1} c$ for $k = 1, 2, \dots$. Then

$$E[L] = \sum_{k \ge 1} k (1-c)^{k-1} c = \frac{1}{c}$$

Equivalently, the sum of survival probabilities $\sum_{t \ge 0} (1-c)^t = 1/c$.

**Where it breaks: mixed populations.** Suppose a share $0.6$ churns at $0.02$ per month and $0.4$ at $0.10$.

- Blended starting churn: $0.6 \times 0.02 + 0.4 \times 0.10 = 0.052$. The formula gives $1/0.052 = 19.2$ months.
- True mean lifetime: $0.6 \times \frac{1}{0.02} + 0.4 \times \frac{1}{0.10} = 30 + 4 = 34$ months (I confirmed by summing the survival curve: 34.0).

The blended churn rate falls over time because high churn customers leave first. This is selection, and it means $1/\text{blended churn}$ underestimates lifetime here (Jensen's inequality: the mean of $1/c$ is above $1/$ the mean of $c$).

**Other ways it breaks**

- Early churn is usually much higher than later churn (the first month is the hardest), so churn is not constant by age.
- Contracts with fixed terms make churn lumpy at renewal dates.
- Right censoring: you rarely observe full lifetimes.

**What to do.** Build survival curves by cohort and by segment, and compute lifetime as the area under the curve over a fixed horizon (for example 24 months) instead of extrapolating one number.
say: If every customer has the same monthly chance c of leaving, the expected lifetime is one over c, so 5 percent churn means 20 months. It breaks when customers differ. Say 60 percent churn at 2 percent a month and 40 percent at 10 percent. Blended churn starts at 5.2 percent, so the formula says 19 months, but the true mean is 0.6 times 50 plus 0.4 times 10, which is 34 months, because the fast churners leave first and the loyal group dominates later. So I prefer survival curves by segment and a fixed horizon over one extrapolated number.

followups.a: High churn customers leave first, so the survivors are increasingly the low churn customers.

followups.a: Cohort survival curves by segment, summed over a fixed horizon such as 24 months.

q: What is growth accounting, and how do you decompose MAU into new, retained, resurrected and churned users?
plain: Growth accounting splits the change in active users into who joined and who left. A user is new if this is their first active period, retained if they were active last period and this one, resurrected if they are active now, were not active last period, but were active before, and churned if they were active last period and not now. With 100,000 MAU at the start, 12,000 new, 3,000 resurrected and 9,000 churned, the end is 106,000, a 6 percent gain. The quick ratio is (12,000 + 3,000) over 9,000, about 1.67.
deep:
**Definitions for period $t$ (month for MAU, day for DAU)**

- **New:** active in $t$ and never active before.
- **Retained:** active in $t-1$ and in $t$.
- **Resurrected:** active in $t$, not in $t-1$, but active at some time before.
- **Churned:** active in $t-1$ and not in $t$.

**Identities**

$$\text{MAU}_t = \text{retained} + \text{new} + \text{resurrected}$$
$$\text{MAU}_{t-1} = \text{retained} + \text{churned}$$

so $\text{MAU}_t - \text{MAU}_{t-1} = \text{new} + \text{resurrected} - \text{churned}$.

**Worked numbers.** Start 100,000. New 12,000, resurrected 3,000, churned 9,000.

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| End MAU | 100,000 + 12,000 + 3,000 - 9,000 = 106,000 |
| Net growth | 6,000 / 100,000 = 6% |
| Quick ratio | (12,000 + 3,000) / 9,000 = 1.67 |

**Reading the quick ratio.** Above 1 the product is growing, and a higher number means growth is cheaper relative to leakage. It describes gains versus losses and does not say whether those gains cost much to acquire.

**Why it helps in a metric drop.** A DAU fall is always a fall in new, retained or resurrected users, or a rise in churn. Growth accounting tells you which one, which narrows the hypothesis list immediately (low new users points to acquisition, low retained points to product or experience, low resurrected points to notifications or email).
say: Growth accounting splits the change in active users into four groups. New users are active for the first time. Retained users were active last period and this one. Resurrected users are active now, were inactive last period, but had been active before. Churned users were active last period and aren't now. So with 100,000 monthly actives, 12,000 new, 3,000 resurrected and 9,000 churned, I end at 106,000, up 6 percent. The quick ratio, gains over losses, is 15,000 over 9,000, about 1.67. It also tells me which bucket to investigate when a metric falls.
must_mention: MAU change equals new plus resurrected minus churned
quick ratio is gains over losses

followups.q: What does a quick ratio below 1 mean?
followups.a: More users are leaving than joining or returning, so active users are shrinking.

followups.q: How does this help diagnose a DAU drop?
followups.a: It shows whether the fall came from fewer new, fewer retained or fewer resurrected users, each pointing to a different cause.

traps: Counting a returning user as new.

q: How do you define churn for a product with no subscription, such as a free app or a marketplace?
plain: With no cancel button, churn is a judgement: you declare a user churned after a period of inactivity. Pick the period from data. Look at the gaps between a user's visits, find the gap length that most returning users stay under, and use something just beyond it. If 95 percent of gaps between visits are under 19 days, declaring churn after 28 days of silence rarely mislabels an active user. Because some churned users come back, count them as resurrected rather than rewriting history.
deep:
**Contractual versus non contractual.** A subscription has an observable cancel event. A free app, a game or a marketplace does not, so churn is inferred.

**Method**

1. For users with at least two active days, compute the gap between consecutive active days.
2. Look at the distribution of those gaps. Choose a threshold near a high percentile (for example the 95th), then round up to a clean number such as a multiple of 7 to keep weekdays balanced.
3. Define churn as "no activity in the last $k$ days" and report the fraction of users in the active base who cross that line each period.
4. Check sensitivity: recompute with $k$ at half and double and see whether conclusions change.

**Product dependent.** A daily game might use 7 days. A marketplace where buyers purchase a few times a year needs far longer, and the activity that counts should be a purchase, not an app open.

**Resurrection.** Some users labelled churned return later. Keep them in growth accounting as resurrected so the inflow is visible, rather than treating the original label as an error.

**Advanced.** For infrequent purchasers, probabilistic models (Pareto/NBD and BG/NBD, known as "buy till you die" models) estimate the probability that a customer is still alive given their purchase history. They are rarely required in a screen but are the standard answer to "what if the gaps are long and irregular?"

In the illustration, if the 95th percentile gap is 19 days, 28 days is a clean multiple of 7 above it. That gap figure is an assumption for illustration, since it depends on the product.
say: With no cancel event, churn is inferred from inactivity, so I pick a threshold from the data. I compute the gaps between a user's consecutive active days, look at a high percentile of that distribution, and round up to a clean number of weeks. For example, if 95 percent of gaps are under 19 days, I'd call someone churned after 28 days of silence. I check sensitivity at half and double that threshold, and I count anyone who comes back as resurrected, not as a labelling mistake. For infrequent buyers I'd count purchases, not app opens.

followups.q: What if purchases are rare and irregular?
followups.a: Use probabilistic models such as BG/NBD that estimate the chance a customer is still active given their history, or use a much longer window on purchases.

followups.q: Why round to whole weeks?
followups.a: To keep the weekday mix balanced so weekday effects do not leak into churn.

traps: Using a one size threshold for products with very different cadences.

q: How do you estimate D30 retention when many recent signups have not yet had 30 days?
plain: Only count users who have had the full 30 days, because the others have not had a chance to be retained and counting them as lost drags the number down. Suppose 100 users sign up each day for 60 days and the true D30 retention is 25 percent. Dividing all retained users by all 6,000 signups gives 12.9 percent, because only 3,100 users are old enough to have a day 30. Restrict to mature cohorts and you recover the true 25 percent. For lifetime curves use Kaplan Meier.
deep:
**The bias.** Recent signups are right censored: they have not reached age 30 yet, so they cannot show a day 30 return. If you divide returns among the old users by all users, the denominator includes people who could not have returned.

**Worked numbers.** 100 signups a day for 60 days, true D30 retention 25%. Users who signed up on day $d$ (counted from the first day) have age $60 - d$ today, so those with $d \le 30$ (31 days of signups, 3,100 users) have reached day 30.

```python
signups_per_day, days, true_d30 = 100, 60, 0.25
mature = sum(1 for d in range(days) if days - d >= 30) * signups_per_day
naive = mature * true_d30 / (signups_per_day * days)
print(mature, round(naive, 3))      # 3100 0.129
```

Naive: $3100 \times 0.25 / 6000 = 12.9\%$. Correct: restrict the denominator to the 3,100 mature users, which gives 25%.

**Rules**

- Report retention only for cohorts old enough, and show the latest immature cohorts as a partial line, clearly marked.
- Never average over cohorts of different maturity.

**Kaplan Meier for permanent churn.** If churn is a one way event (a cancellation), estimate survival with

$$\hat S(t) = \prod_{t_i \le t} \left(1 - \frac{d_i}{n_i}\right)$$

where $d_i$ is the number who churn at time $t_i$ and $n_i$ is the number still at risk (not yet churned and not yet censored). Censored users stay in the denominator until their last observed time, then leave it.

**Caveat.** Retention defined as "active on day N" is not a survival function because users can come back. Kaplan Meier fits when churn is defined as permanent, such as cancellation or a long inactivity threshold.
say: Recent signups haven't had 30 days yet, so they can't show a day 30 return, and counting them in the denominator drags retention down. In an example with 100 signups a day for 60 days and a true rate of 25 percent, dividing all retained users by all 6,000 signups gives 12.9 percent, because only 3,100 users are old enough. I restrict to mature cohorts and get the true 25 percent. For churn defined as permanent, like cancellation, I'd use a Kaplan Meier survival estimate, which handles censored users properly.

followups.q: When does Kaplan Meier not fit?
followups.a: When 'retained' means active on day N, because users can leave and return, so it is not a one way survival event.

followups.q: How would you show the newest cohort?
followups.a: As a partial line, marked as immature, never averaged with mature cohorts.

traps: Dividing by all signups regardless of how old they are.

q: What is a good retention rate?
plain: There is no universal good number. It depends on how often the product is naturally used, so a daily social app and a yearly tax product have very different healthy levels. A better answer compares three things: the shape of your curve (does it flatten at a plateau), the trend across your own cohorts (are newer cohorts better), and similar products at the same frequency. For example, 30 percent day 30 retention is excellent for a product used a few times a year and worrying for a messenger. Say what you would measure, not a number.
deep:
**The answer interviewers want:** it depends, and here is how I would judge it.

1. **Natural frequency.** Choose a retention definition that matches it. Daily products use day N, weekly products use week N, infrequent products use month or quarter retention on a core action.
2. **Shape.** A curve that flattens means a durable core exists. A curve heading to zero is a leaky bucket whatever the level is today.
3. **Trend.** Compare cohort over cohort at the same age. Improvement matters more than the level.
4. **Segments.** Retention among users acquired through a channel or reaching the activation event is more informative than the blend.
5. **Comparables.** Public benchmark numbers exist but vary by source, category and definition, so use them only as a rough sanity check for similar products and with the same retention definition. I have not verified any specific benchmark here, so I do not quote one.
6. **Economics.** The real test is whether retention supports payback: does lifetime margin exceed acquisition cost (see unit economics).

**Example.** 30% day 30 retention: worrying for a messenger where users should be daily, excellent for an annual tax product measured on repeat in the next season. The number is meaningless without the cadence.
say: I'd say there's no universal good number, because it depends on how often the product is naturally used. A daily messenger and a yearly tax product have very different healthy levels. So I judge it on three things. Does the curve flatten at a plateau or head to zero. Are newer cohorts retaining better than older ones at the same age. And how do we compare with similar products at the same frequency. Then I tie it to economics, whether lifetime margin pays back acquisition cost. Thirty percent at day 30 could be excellent or worrying depending on the product.

followups.q: What if the interviewer insists on a number?
followups.a: Give a range tied to a stated cadence and say it is a rough check, not a target. Then explain what you would compare against internally.

followups.q: Which matters more, level or trend?
followups.a: Trend across cohorts and the existence of a plateau, because the level depends on cadence and definition.

traps: Quoting a universal benchmark with no mention of cadence or definition.

q: How would you extrapolate lifetime value from only six months of retention data?
plain: Fit a model of how retention decays and project it, instead of extending the last month's churn. The shifted beta geometric model assumes each customer has their own churn probability, so the early leavers go first and the blended churn rate falls over time. Fitted to six months of survival (100, 70, 56, 48, 43 and 39 percent), it predicts about 25.7 percent still active at month 12, against 19.7 percent if you keep the last month's 9.3 percent churn going. Then check the method on older cohorts whose later months you already know.
deep:
**Why a model.** Constant churn extrapolation uses the latest churn rate forever. Real cohorts have falling churn, because heterogeneous customers sort themselves: those likely to leave do so early.

**Shifted beta geometric (sBG) model** (Fader and Hardie). Each customer has a churn probability $\theta$ drawn from a Beta($\alpha$, $\beta$) distribution, and churns each period with that probability. Then

$$S(t) = \frac{B(\alpha, \beta + t)}{B(\alpha, \beta)}, \qquad r(t) = \frac{S(t)}{S(t-1)} = \frac{\beta + t - 1}{\alpha + \beta + t - 1}$$

with $B$ the beta function. The retention rate $r(t)$ rises with $t$, so the churn rate falls, as in real data.

**Fit and project (illustrative data).** Survival at months 0 to 5: 1.00, 0.70, 0.56, 0.48, 0.43, 0.39. Least squares on $S(t)$ (maximum likelihood on cohort counts is the better practice).

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from scipy.special import betaln

observed = np.array([1.00, 0.70, 0.56, 0.48, 0.43, 0.39])       # share of a cohort still subscribed, months 0 to 5
t_obs = np.arange(len(observed))

def survival(t, alpha, beta):
    return np.exp(betaln(alpha, beta + t) - betaln(alpha, beta))   # shifted beta geometric survival

def loss(params):
    a, b = np.exp(params)
    return ((survival(t_obs[1:], a, b) - observed[1:]) ** 2).sum()

fit = minimize(loss, x0=np.log([1.0, 3.0]), method="Nelder-Mead")
alpha, beta = np.exp(fit.x)
print("alpha, beta", round(alpha, 2), round(beta, 2))
for t in (6, 12, 24):
    print("month", t, "predicted survival", round(float(survival(t, alpha, beta)), 3))
last_churn = 1 - observed[-1] / observed[-2]
print("constant churn extrapolation at month 12:", round(float(observed[-1] * (1 - last_churn) ** 7), 3))
print("expected months retained in first 24 (sum of S(0..23)):", round(float(survival(np.arange(24), alpha, beta).sum()), 1))
```

| Quantity | sBG fit | Constant churn from the last month |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Month 12 survival | 25.7% | 19.7% |
| Month 24 survival | 18.1% | 6.1% (0.39 x 0.907^19) |

The fitted parameters are $\alpha = 0.54$, $\beta = 1.23$. Summing $S(t)$ for the first 24 months gives 8.0 expected paid months per subscriber. Multiply by margin per month for a 24 month LTV (and discount if needed).

**Checks before trusting it**

1. **Backtest.** Fit on the first 6 months of older cohorts and compare with their actual month 12 and 24.
2. **Stability.** Six points can give a loose fit. Use several cohorts and report a range.
3. **Contractual churn only.** This model needs an observable end event (cancellation). For non contractual customers (irregular purchases), the related BG/NBD family applies.
4. **Cohort differences.** Fit by channel or plan if they differ.

**Interview line.** "I would not extend the last month's churn. I would fit a heterogeneity model, check it on older cohorts, and quote the range."

The data are made up for illustration. The fit was run with the code above.
say: I'd fit a model of how retention decays instead of extending the last month's churn forever. The shifted beta geometric model gives each customer their own churn probability, so early leavers go first and blended churn falls over time. Fitted to six months of survival, 100, 70, 56, 48, 43 and 39 percent, it predicts about 25.7 percent still active at month 12, versus 19.7 percent if I keep the last month's churn going. Then I'd backtest on older cohorts whose later months are known, and quote a range.
must_mention: fit a decay model, not constant churn

followups.q: Why is constant churn extrapolation too pessimistic here?
followups.a: Churn falls as the high churn customers leave, so keeping the latest rate fixed understates later survival.

followups.q: What changes for a free app with no cancellation event?
followups.a: There is no observable end, so use a non contractual model such as BG/NBD or define churn by inactivity.

q: What are ARPU and ARPPU, and how do they relate to the paying rate?
plain: ARPU is average revenue per user, revenue divided by all users in a period. ARPPU is average revenue per paying user, revenue divided by paying users only. The paying rate is paying users over all users, and ARPU equals paying rate times ARPPU. With USD 500,000 revenue, 400,000 monthly users and 20,000 payers, ARPU is USD 1.25, ARPPU is USD 25 and the paying rate is 5 percent, and 0.05 times 25 is 1.25. The split shows whether revenue grew because more people paid or because payers paid more.
deep:
**Definitions** (state the period and the user base each time)

$$\text{ARPU} = \frac{\text{revenue}}{\text{users}}, \qquad \text{ARPPU} = \frac{\text{revenue}}{\text{paying users}}, \qquad \text{paying rate} = \frac{\text{paying users}}{\text{users}}$$

$$\text{ARPU} = \text{paying rate} \times \text{ARPPU}$$

**Worked numbers.** Revenue USD 500,000, MAU 400,000, payers 20,000.

| Metric | Calculation | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ARPU | 500,000 / 400,000 | USD 1.25 |
| ARPPU | 500,000 / 20,000 | USD 25 |
| Paying rate | 20,000 / 400,000 | 5% |
| Check | 0.05 x 25 | USD 1.25 |

**Decomposing a change.** Growth rates multiply: $(1+g_{\text{ARPU}}) = (1+g_{\text{rate}})(1+g_{\text{ARPPU}})$. If the paying rate rises 8% and ARPPU rises 2%, ARPU rises $1.08 \times 1.02 - 1 = 10.2\%$.

**Pitfalls**

- **Denominator choice.** Registered users, monthly actives and daily actives give very different ARPU. ARPDAU (revenue per daily active user) is common in games.
- **Skew.** In freemium products a few heavy spenders dominate ARPPU. Report the median payer and the spend distribution.
- **Period mismatch.** Annual revenue over monthly users is a classic error.
- **Revenue is not profit.** ARPU ignores cost to serve.
say: ARPU is revenue per user across everyone, ARPPU is revenue per paying user, and the paying rate is the share of users who pay. They tie together exactly: ARPU equals paying rate times ARPPU. With 500,000 dollars of revenue, 400,000 monthly users and 20,000 payers, ARPU is 1.25 dollars, ARPPU is 25 dollars, and the paying rate is 5 percent. I use the split to see whether a revenue change came from more people paying or from each payer paying more, and I report the median payer because heavy spenders skew ARPPU.

ARPU equals paying rate times ARPPU

q: What is the difference between GMV, revenue and take rate in a marketplace?
plain: GMV, gross merchandise volume, is the total value of sales that flow through the marketplace. Revenue is the part the marketplace keeps, typically as fees. Take rate is revenue divided by GMV. If a rides marketplace has USD 50 million of GMV and a 20 percent take rate, gross revenue is USD 10 million. If it pays USD 3 million in driver incentives that count against revenue, net revenue is USD 7 million and the effective take rate is 14 percent. Quoting GMV as if it were revenue overstates the business several times over.
deep:
**Definitions** (following the a16z startup metrics article)

- **GMV:** total dollar volume of sales through the marketplace in a period. Annualising a recent month or quarter gives a run rate.
- **Revenue:** the part of GMV the marketplace keeps, usually transaction fees plus advertising or sponsorship. It is typically a fraction of GMV.
- **Take rate:** revenue / GMV (the article implies this ratio without naming it).

**Worked example**

| Line | Value |
| --- | --- |
| GMV | USD 50,000,000 |
| Take rate (gross) | 20% |
| Gross revenue | USD 10,000,000 |
| Driver incentives (contra revenue) | USD 3,000,000 |
| Net revenue | USD 7,000,000 |
| Effective take rate | 7 / 50 = 14% |

**Why it matters**

- Growth in GMV can come with a falling take rate (discounts, incentives, mix shift to low fee categories), so GMV growth alone does not mean revenue growth.
- **Principal versus agent.** Accounting rules decide whether a business reports the full sale (principal) or only its fee (agent). Two companies with the same economics can report revenue that differs by a factor of five, so compare on a like for like basis.
- Decompose revenue growth: $\text{revenue} = \text{GMV} \times \text{take rate}$, and GMV itself is orders times average order value.
say: GMV is the total value of goods or rides sold through the marketplace, revenue is the share the marketplace keeps, and take rate is revenue divided by GMV. With 50 million dollars of GMV and a 20 percent take rate, gross revenue is 10 million. If 3 million goes to driver incentives booked against revenue, net revenue is 7 million and the effective take rate is 14 percent. So I never treat GMV growth as revenue growth. I decompose revenue into GMV times take rate, and I watch for accounting differences between reporting gross and net.

take rate is revenue over GMV

followups.q: GMV grew 30 percent and revenue grew 10 percent. Why?
followups.a: The take rate fell, from discounts, incentives or a mix shift toward lower fee categories. Decompose revenue into GMV times take rate.

followups.q: Why can two marketplaces with the same economics report different revenue?
followups.a: One may report gross sales as principal and the other only its fee as agent.

q: What is the difference between gross margin and contribution margin?
plain: Gross margin is revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the product, such as hosting and support, shown as a percent of revenue. Contribution margin goes further and subtracts every cost that varies with each customer or order, including payment fees, commissions and account management. For a software customer paying USD 100 a month with USD 20 of hosting and support, gross margin is USD 80, or 80 percent. After USD 20 of other variable costs, contribution margin is USD 60, or 60 percent. Contribution margin is the number that decides whether growing is worth it.
deep:
**Definitions**

- **Gross margin** = revenue - cost of goods sold (costs tied to producing and delivering the product or service, including support, which varies by company). The a16z article stresses that the right list varies by business.
- **Contribution margin per customer per month** = revenue from the customer - the variable costs of serving them, including selling, administrative and operational costs that scale with the customer.

**Worked example (software customer, per month)**

| Line | USD |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue | 100 |
| Hosting | 12 |
| Support | 8 |
| **Gross margin** | **80 (80%)** |
| Payment fees | 3 |
| Sales commission (amortised) | 10 |
| Account management | 7 |
| **Contribution margin** | **60 (60%)** |

**Why contribution margin drives decisions.** It is the money each additional customer adds toward fixed costs and profit. Lifetime value, payback and the LTV to CAC ratio should be built on contribution margin, not revenue. Using revenue overstates value (for the numbers above, 100 versus 60 per month).

**Fixed versus variable.** Salaries of a fixed team, rent and R and D are not in contribution margin. They are covered by the total contribution across all customers.
say: Gross margin is revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the product, like hosting and support. Contribution margin subtracts every cost that scales with each customer or order, so it also takes out things like payment fees, commissions and account management. A software customer paying 100 dollars a month with 20 dollars of hosting and support has an 80 percent gross margin, and if there's another 20 dollars of variable cost the contribution margin is 60 percent. I build lifetime value and payback on contribution margin, because it's what each extra customer actually adds.

contribution margin subtracts all variable cost

q: What is CAC, and what is the difference between blended and paid CAC?
plain: Customer acquisition cost is the total cost of acquiring new customers divided by the number acquired. Blended CAC divides total acquisition spend by all new customers, including organic ones. Paid CAC divides the spend by only the customers the paid channels brought in. With USD 200,000 of spend and 2,000 new customers, blended CAC is USD 100. If only 800 of them came from paid channels, paid CAC is USD 250. Investors and finance teams trust paid CAC more, because organic customers flatter the blend.
deep:
**Definitions** (following the a16z article)

- **CAC** = full cost of acquiring a user, per user, including referral fees, credits and discounts as well as marketing spend.
- **Blended CAC** = total acquisition cost / total new customers from all channels, including organic.
- **Paid CAC** = total acquisition cost / new customers from paid marketing.

The article says investors weight paid CAC more heavily, and that blended CAC is only meaningful if you can show paid spend actually drives organic growth.

**Worked numbers.** Spend USD 200,000. New customers 2,000, of which 800 came from paid channels.

$$\text{blended CAC} = \frac{200{,}000}{2{,}000} = 100, \qquad \text{paid CAC} = \frac{200{,}000}{800} = 250$$

**What to include (fully loaded CAC).** Ad spend, agency fees, the sales and marketing team's cost, tooling, referral rewards and signup discounts. Leaving out salaries is the most common way CAC gets flattered.

**Other points**

- **By channel.** Compute CAC per channel and compare with LTV per channel.
- **Marginal versus average.** The next dollar of spend usually buys customers at a higher cost than the average dollar, because the cheapest audiences are used first. Decisions about scaling spend need marginal CAC.
- **Attribution.** CAC by channel depends on the attribution model (see funnels and attribution).
say: CAC is the full cost of acquiring new customers divided by how many you got. Blended CAC divides total spend by all new customers including organic ones, while paid CAC divides it by just the customers paid channels delivered. With 200,000 dollars spent and 2,000 new customers, blended is 100 dollars, but if only 800 came from paid it's 250 dollars. Finance trusts paid CAC more, because organic customers flatter the blend. I also include salaries and discounts in the cost, and I look at marginal CAC when deciding whether to scale a channel.

followups.q: What is marginal CAC and why does it matter?
followups.a: The cost of the next customer. It usually rises as spend grows, so average CAC understates the cost of scaling.

followups.q: When is blended CAC meaningful?
followups.a: Only if paid spend demonstrably drives organic growth, for example through brand or referral effects.

traps: Leaving salaries and discounts out of CAC.

q: How do you compute customer lifetime value, and what does LTV to CAC tell you?
plain: Lifetime value is the contribution margin a customer is expected to bring over their life with you. With constant churn, it is monthly contribution margin divided by monthly churn. A customer paying USD 30 a month with USD 12 of variable cost leaves USD 18 of margin. At 4 percent monthly churn the expected life is 25 months, so LTV is USD 450. If CAC is USD 150, LTV to CAC is 3. Using revenue instead of margin gives USD 750 and overstates value by two thirds.
deep:
**Formula** (a16z version: LTV is the present value of future net profit, not revenue)

$$\text{LTV} = \text{contribution margin per month} \times \text{average lifespan in months} = m \times \frac{1}{c}$$

with $m$ the monthly contribution margin and $c$ the monthly churn.

**Worked numbers.**

| Quantity | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue per month | USD 30 |
| Variable cost per month | USD 12 |
| Contribution margin $m$ | USD 18 (60%) |
| Monthly churn $c$ | 4% |
| Average lifespan $1/c$ | 25 months |
| LTV | 18 x 25 = USD 450 |
| CAC | USD 150 |
| LTV to CAC | 3.0 |
| Revenue based LTV (wrong) | 30 x 25 = USD 750, which is 1.67 times too high |

**Reading LTV to CAC.** It says how many dollars of lifetime margin each acquisition dollar buys. Around 3 is a commonly quoted rule of thumb for a healthy business, but the right level depends on payback time, churn certainty and capital cost. It is a heuristic, not a law.

**Limits**

- Constant churn is a simplification (see the card on lifetime and heterogeneity).
- With a short history, measure realised 12 and 24 month LTV by cohort instead of projecting. The a16z article makes the same suggestion.
- LTV ignores the time value of money (the discounted version follows).
say: Lifetime value is the contribution margin a customer is expected to bring over their life. With constant churn it's monthly margin divided by monthly churn. A customer paying 30 dollars with 12 of variable cost leaves 18 a month, and at 4 percent churn the expected life is 25 months, so LTV is 450 dollars. If CAC is 150, LTV to CAC is 3. Using revenue instead of margin would say 750 and overstate value by two thirds. The caveats are that churn isn't constant, and with a short history I'd rather measure realised 12 and 24 month value by cohort.

followups.q: Is an LTV to CAC of 3 always the target?
followups.a: No. It is a rule of thumb. Payback time, churn uncertainty and cost of capital change what is acceptable.

followups.q: What if you only have six months of data?
followups.a: Report realised value by cohort over the observed period rather than extrapolating a lifetime from early churn.

traps: Computing LTV from revenue.
Treating the 3 to 1 heuristic as a hard rule.

q: What is CAC payback period, and why can the simple formula be too optimistic?
plain: CAC payback is how many months of a customer's contribution margin it takes to earn back what you paid to acquire them. With a CAC of USD 150 and USD 18 of monthly margin, the simple answer is 150 divided by 18, about 8.3 months. That ignores customers who leave before paying back. With 4 percent monthly churn, expected margin in the first 8 months is only USD 125, and the cohort does not break even until about month 10, nearly 10 months, not 8.3.
deep:
**Simple formula**

$$\text{payback (months)} = \frac{\text{CAC}}{\text{monthly contribution margin per customer}} = \frac{150}{18} = 8.33$$

**Churn adjusted payback.** Not every customer lasts that long. With monthly churn $c$ and margin collected at the start of each month, expected cumulative margin per acquired customer after $n$ months is

$$m \sum_{t=0}^{n-1} (1-c)^t = m \,\frac{1 - (1-c)^n}{c}$$

Set it equal to CAC and solve for $n$:

$$n = \frac{\ln\left(1 - \frac{\text{CAC}\cdot c}{m}\right)}{\ln(1-c)} = \frac{\ln(1 - 150 \times 0.04 / 18)}{\ln 0.96} = 9.93 \text{ months}$$

Check: after 8 months expected margin is $18 \times (1 - 0.96^8)/0.04 = 125.4$, below 150. If $\text{CAC} \cdot c / m \ge 1$, payback never happens at all (here the limit is CAC of 450, which equals LTV).

**Rules of thumb.** Finance teams often want payback inside a year or so, with the target depending on capital cost and how certain retention is. Treat any single target as a heuristic.

**Variants.** Gross margin payback uses gross margin instead of contribution margin and flatters the result. Revenue payback is flatter still. Say which you mean. For a marketplace, payback is often measured in orders, not months.
say: CAC payback is how long it takes a customer's margin to earn back what you paid to acquire them. With a CAC of 150 dollars and 18 dollars of monthly margin, the simple answer is 150 over 18, about 8.3 months. But that treats every customer as staying, and some leave first. At 4 percent monthly churn the expected cumulative margin after eight months is only about 125 dollars, and the cohort doesn't actually break even until nearly 10 months. So I compute payback on a survival adjusted basis, and I say whether it uses contribution margin or the more flattering gross margin.

followups.q: When does payback never happen?
followups.a: When CAC times churn is at least the monthly margin, which means CAC is at or above LTV.

followups.q: Margin or revenue for payback?
followups.a: Contribution margin. Gross margin or revenue flatter the number.

traps: Using the simple formula for a high churn product.

q: How do you include discounting in LTV?
plain: Discounting says a dollar later is worth less than a dollar now, so you weight each month's expected margin by both the chance the customer is still there and a discount factor. With constant churn c and monthly discount rate d, LTV becomes margin times (1 + d) divided by (c + d). For USD 18 margin, 4 percent churn and 1 percent monthly discounting, LTV is USD 363.60, not USD 450. The higher the discount rate, the more weight lands on the early months and the lower LTV falls.
deep:
**Derivation.** Margin $m$ is collected at the start of each month while the customer remains. The probability of being a customer in month $t$ is $(1-c)^t$ and the discount factor is $(1+d)^{-t}$. So

$$\text{LTV} = m \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1-c}{1+d}\right)^t = \frac{m}{1 - \frac{1-c}{1+d}} = m\,\frac{1+d}{c+d}$$

**Numbers.** $m = 18$, $c = 0.04$:

- $d = 0$: $18/0.04 = 450$.
- $d = 0.01$ (about 12.7% a year, since $1.01^{12} - 1 = 0.1268$): $18 \times 1.01 / 0.05 = 363.6$. Summing the series numerically also gives 363.6.

```python
def ltv(monthly_revenue, monthly_variable_cost, monthly_churn, monthly_discount=0.0):
    margin = monthly_revenue - monthly_variable_cost
    return margin * (1 + monthly_discount) / (monthly_churn + monthly_discount)

print(round(ltv(30, 12, 0.04), 1))          # 450.0
print(round(ltv(30, 12, 0.04, 0.01), 1))    # 363.6
```

**Reading it.** Discounting cuts LTV by 19% here. The effect is larger when churn is low (long lifetimes are discounted more) and when the discount rate is high.

**Practical notes**

- The discount rate is a company choice, often tied to the cost of capital. State it.
- A cleaner empirical alternative is to cap the horizon, for example report realised 24 month margin per acquired customer.
- If margin per customer grows with tenure (expansion revenue), add a growth term: with margin growth $g$ per month the denominator becomes roughly $c + d - g$ when $g$ is small, and diverges if $g \ge c + d$, so cap the horizon.
say: Discounting weights each future month's margin by both the chance the customer is still around and a factor for the time value of money. With constant churn c and monthly discount rate d, LTV is margin times one plus d, divided by c plus d. For 18 dollars of margin and 4 percent churn, LTV is 450 undiscounted, but with 1 percent monthly discounting, about 12.7 percent a year, it's 363.60. That's roughly 19 percent lower. Higher discount rates and lower churn both increase the haircut, so I state the rate I used, or I just cap the horizon at 24 months.

followups.a: Their value sits further in the future, where the discount factor is smaller.

followups.a: Report realised or expected margin over a fixed horizon, such as 24 months.

q: What are net dollar retention and gross dollar retention, and how do they differ?
plain: Net dollar retention (NDR) measures how much recurring revenue a group of existing customers generates now compared with a year ago, including upsell, downgrades and cancellations, and excluding new customers. Gross dollar retention (GDR) leaves expansion out and can never exceed 100 percent. Starting with USD 1,000,000, with USD 80,000 of expansion, USD 20,000 of downgrades and USD 50,000 of cancellations, NDR is 101 percent and GDR is 93 percent. NDR above 100 means the base grows even with no new customers.
deep:
**Definitions** for a cohort of customers measured from a start date to an end date (often 12 months), excluding customers who joined after the start:

$$\text{NDR} = \frac{\text{start MRR} + \text{expansion} - \text{contraction} - \text{churn}}{\text{start MRR}}, \qquad \text{GDR} = \frac{\text{start MRR} - \text{contraction} - \text{churn}}{\text{start MRR}}$$

NDR equals one minus net dollar churn, using the a16z definition of net dollar churn as (revenue lost - revenue gained from expansion) / starting revenue (the article does not name NDR itself).

**Worked numbers.** Start USD 1,000,000, expansion USD 80,000, contraction USD 20,000, cancellations USD 50,000.

| Metric | Calculation | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NDR | (1,000,000 + 80,000 - 20,000 - 50,000) / 1,000,000 | 101% |
| GDR | (1,000,000 - 20,000 - 50,000) / 1,000,000 | 93% |
| Net dollar churn | (70,000 - 80,000) / 1,000,000 | -1% |

**How to use them together.** GDR is the leaky bucket measure: how much the product loses. NDR adds how much the survivors grow. A business with GDR 93% and NDR 101% is leaking 7% but refilling it through expansion, which depends on a few expanding accounts. Check concentration: if two large accounts supply most expansion, NDR is fragile.

**Caveat on blending.** As the a16z article notes about net churn, expansion can hide customer losses, so always read NDR next to logo churn and GDR.
say: Net dollar retention is how much recurring revenue today's cohort of existing customers produces compared with a year ago, including upsell, downgrades and cancellations, but excluding new customers. Gross dollar retention leaves out expansion, so it can't exceed 100 percent. Starting from a million dollars, with 80,000 of expansion, 20,000 of downgrades and 50,000 of cancellations, NDR is 101 percent and GDR is 93 percent. I read them together: GDR shows the leak, NDR shows whether expansion refills it, and I check whether a few big accounts are driving the expansion.

GDR excludes expansion, capped at 100 percent
101 percent and 93 percent in the example
